options.a: Lower both side rails and raise the bed to working height, then step away to collect clean linen
options.b: Fanfold the soiled linen toward the patient and lay the clean linen on top of the dirty roll
options.c: Keep the patient covered and use side rails/safety measures while changing linen
options.d: Remove the top sheet and bath blanket first so the bottom sheet is easier to reach on each side

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving rails down with the bed raised while stepping away creates a fall risk; gather linen first and stay at the bedside.
distractorExplanations.b: Clean linen must not touch soiled linen; roll soiled linen inward and keep clean linen separate to avoid cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing the top covers first exposes the patient; a bath blanket stays over the patient throughout occupied bedmaking.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-00.explanation: Dignity, warmth, and skin protection matter during occupied bedmaking. Follow facility policy on side rails and safety measures.

options.a: Oral fluids and urine, while IV fluids and wound drainage are recorded only on the MAR
options.b: Meal percentages, oral fluids, and estimated urine volume when the patient voids in the toilet
options.c: Oral fluids, urine, and daily weight, with emesis and liquid stool left out of output totals
options.d: Oral fluids, IV fluids as applicable, urine, and other measurable outputs per protocol

distractorExplanations.a: I&O totals include IV fluids and measurable drainage; leaving them off the I&O sheet makes the fluid balance inaccurate.
distractorExplanations.b: Urine is measured with a toilet hat or graduate, not estimated; meal percentages are a nutrition record, not I&O.
distractorExplanations.c: Emesis and liquid stool are measurable outputs that belong in I&O; daily weight is recorded on a separate flow sheet.

options.a: Head of bed elevated (commonly 45–60°) for comfort/breathing/eating
options.b: Head of bed flat with the patient on the back and knees slightly flexed
options.c: Patient lying on the left side with the right knee drawn up toward the chest
options.d: Head of bed lowered below the level of the feet to improve venous return

distractorExplanations.b: Lying flat on the back with knees flexed is dorsal recumbent/supine positioning, not the head-elevated Fowler's position.
distractorExplanations.c: Left side-lying with the upper knee flexed is Sims' position, used for enemas and rectal procedures, not Fowler's.
distractorExplanations.d: Head lower than the feet is Trendelenburg position; Fowler's raises the head of the bed instead of lowering it.

options.a: Position the patient semi-reclined at 30° and alternate large bites with sips of thin liquid
options.b: Keep head elevated, offer small bites, and ensure swallowing before next bite
options.c: Offer thin liquids through a straw between bites to help the food go down faster
options.d: Lay the patient flat for 30 minutes after the meal so the food settles before activity

distractorExplanations.a: Aspiration precautions need upright positioning (about 90°) and small bites; 30° with thin-liquid washes raises aspiration risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Straws and thin liquids speed flow and increase aspiration risk; follow the ordered liquid consistency and pace slowly.
distractorExplanations.d: Patients at aspiration risk stay upright for about 30 minutes after meals; lying flat promotes reflux and aspiration.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-00.explanation: Aspiration precautions require positioning and pacing; report coughing/wet voice. Follow the facility's aspiration protocol and ordered diet texture.

options.a: Hanging the drainage bag on the bed's side rail so it moves with the patient when rails go up
options.b: Disconnecting the catheter from the tubing to empty the bag faster when it is nearly full
options.c: Keeping the drainage bag below bladder level and peri-care without kinking tubing
options.d: Placing the drainage bag on the floor beside the bed so gravity drainage works best

distractorExplanations.a: Bags hang on the bed frame, not side rails; raising the rail can lift the bag above the bladder and pull on the catheter.
distractorExplanations.b: The closed system stays connected; the bag is emptied through its drain spout, since breaking the junction invites infection.
distractorExplanations.d: The bag must stay below the bladder but off the floor; floor contact contaminates the bag and its drain spout.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-00.explanation: Closed system and gravity drainage reduce UTI risk; never use bag for drinking water. Perform peri-care per protocol.

options.a: Massaging reddened areas over bony prominences to restore circulation
options.b: Repositioning every 4 hours and keeping the head of bed above 45° at rest
options.c: Placing a donut-shaped cushion under the sacrum to lift it off the mattress
options.d: Repositioning on schedule, skin inspection, and keeping skin clean/dry

distractorExplanations.a: Massaging reddened bony prominences can deepen tissue damage; reddened areas should be offloaded and reported instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Turning is usually at least every 2 hours, and HOB above 30° increases sacral shear; 4 hours and >45° raise injury risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Donut cushions concentrate pressure on the ring edges and reduce blood flow; pressure-redistribution surfaces are preferred.

options.a: Balance/zero the scale, assist safely, and record with footwear standards per policy
options.b: Weigh the patient at a different time each day so readings reflect normal daily variation
options.c: Have the patient keep shoes and a coat on, then subtract an estimated 5 pounds afterward
options.d: Let the patient steady themselves by holding the wall rail while the reading is taken

distractorExplanations.b: Daily weights use the same time, scale, and clothing; changing the time adds variation that masks true fluid changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracting an estimate for clothing is inaccurate; weights use consistent minimal clothing with the scale zeroed beforehand.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaning on a rail shifts weight off the scale and gives a falsely low reading; unsteady patients need a chair or bed scale.

options.a: Supine flat position, a full cup of water to rinse, and a toothbrush to clean the gums
options.b: Lateral position, suction available, and gentle mouth care to prevent aspiration
options.c: High-Fowler's position, mouthwash rinse by syringe, and mouth care once every 24 hours
options.d: Lateral position with lemon-glycerin swabs used repeatedly to keep the mucosa moist

distractorExplanations.a: Flat positioning and pouring rinse water into an unconscious patient's mouth risk aspiration; use side-lying and minimal fluid.
distractorExplanations.c: Unconscious patients need frequent oral care (often every 2 hours) with minimal fluid; syringe rinses can be aspirated.
distractorExplanations.d: Lemon-glycerin swabs dry and irritate the mucosa and erode tooth enamel; they are discouraged for routine oral care.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-01.explanation: Airway protection is critical during unconscious oral hygiene. Position and suction follow facility protocol.

options.a: Use whichever scale is closest each day and record the reading in the nurse's notes later
options.b: Weigh the patient after breakfast one day and before breakfast the next to average intake
options.c: Zero/balance the scale, have the patient wear similar clothing/shoes, and record accurately
options.d: Round each reading to the nearest 5 pounds so trends are easier to compare between shifts

distractorExplanations.a: Serial weights require the same scale each time and prompt charting; switching scales introduces device-to-device error.
distractorExplanations.b: Weights are taken at the same time daily, usually before breakfast after voiding; alternating times distorts fluid trends.
distractorExplanations.d: Rounding to 5 pounds hides clinically important 1–2 pound fluid shifts; record the exact reading in the ordered unit.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-01.explanation: Accurate weights guide fluid/medication decisions; technique matters. Clothing and footwear follow the facility weighing protocol.

options.a: Fluid overload from thickened liquids
options.b: Urinary retention after meals
options.c: Choking only on solid foods, not liquids
options.d: Aspiration during eating/drinking

distractorExplanations.a: Thickened liquids slow swallowing to reduce aspiration; dysphagia patients are more at risk of dehydration than fluid overload.
distractorExplanations.b: Urinary retention is not linked to swallowing difficulty; the key danger of dysphagia is food or fluid entering the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Thin liquids are often the hardest to control and the most likely to be aspirated; the risk is not limited to solid foods.

options.a: Use two identifiers (e.g., name and date of birth) and match the wristband/order
options.b: Ask 'Are you Mr. Smith?' and confirm the name on the door card before starting care
options.c: Use the room and bed number plus the patient's name as written on the whiteboard
options.d: Check the wristband name only, since the band was verified by staff at admission

distractorExplanations.b: Leading yes/no questions and door cards are unreliable; ask the patient to state name and DOB and check the wristband.
distractorExplanations.c: Room and bed numbers are not patient identifiers because patients move; use two person-specific identifiers like name and DOB.
distractorExplanations.d: One identifier is not enough even from a wristband; national patient safety goals require two identifiers before each task.

options.a: Keep the bed at its lowest height while working and turn the patient without asking for help
options.b: Maintain side-rail safety, keep the patient covered, and use good body mechanics
options.c: Raise both side rails while working so the patient cannot roll in either direction
options.d: Shake out the soiled sheets at the bedside to clear crumbs before rolling them up

distractorExplanations.a: The bed is raised to working height during care to protect your back, then lowered when finished; get help for dependent patients.
distractorExplanations.c: The far rail is up but the working-side rail is lowered while you are there; keeping both up blocks care and can act as a restraint.
distractorExplanations.d: Shaking soiled linen disperses microorganisms into the room; roll soiled linen inward, away from your uniform.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-01.explanation: Occupied bedmaking prioritizes safety, privacy, and ergonomics; get help for dependent patients. Covering the patient protects dignity and warmth.

options.a: Briskly and past the point of resistance so the joint gains new range each session
options.b: Holding the limb by the muscle belly and moving several joints together for speed
options.c: As ordered, supporting joints, and stopping if pain/resistance indicates harm
options.d: Once weekly with the patient lying prone, starting at the feet and working upward

distractorExplanations.a: ROM is slow and gentle and stops at resistance or pain; forcing past it can tear tissue or dislocate a joint.
distractorExplanations.b: Joints are supported above and below and moved one at a time; grabbing the muscle belly and combining joints risks injury.
distractorExplanations.d: ROM is usually done at least daily (often with bathing) with the patient supine, working head to toe; weekly prone sessions are wrong.

options.a: Clean dentures over an empty sink, then store them dry in a tissue on the overbed table
options.b: Rinse the dentures under hot running water, then return them to the mouth immediately
options.c: Hold the dentures in bare hands over the sink while brushing them with regular toothpaste
options.d: Handle dentures carefully and keep them in a labeled container with water/solution

distractorExplanations.a: Clean over a towel-lined or water-filled sink to cushion drops and store in a labeled cup; tissue-wrapped dentures get thrown out.
distractorExplanations.b: Hot water can warp dentures; use cool or lukewarm water, and the mouth also needs care before the dentures go back in.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves are required, and abrasive regular toothpaste can scratch dentures; use denture cleanser over a padded sink.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-01.explanation: Dentures are costly and easily misplaced; labeled containers and proper solution protect the patient. Follow policy on the soaking solution, and prevent loss or breakage.

options.a: A clean, warm, dry finger with minimal nail polish per manufacturer/protocol
options.b: The same arm as the blood pressure cuff so both readings can be taken at once
options.c: A finger with an acrylic nail, after confirming the patient's hand is resting still
options.d: The earlobe for every adult, because finger readings run several points too high

distractorExplanations.b: Cuff inflation cuts off blood flow and makes SpO2 drop or read erratically; place the probe on the opposite arm.
distractorExplanations.c: Artificial and acrylic nails block the light path and cause false readings; remove them or choose another site.
distractorExplanations.d: Earlobe probes are an alternative when finger perfusion is poor, not a universal default; finger readings are not systematically high.

options.a: Provide privacy, lower the head of bed flat, and leave the patient on the pan for 30 minutes
options.b: Provide privacy, position the pan under the hips, and ensure the call light is within reach
options.c: Warm the pan, roll the patient away, and place the pan at the lower back above the hips
options.d: Remove gloves after placing the pan, then handle the used pan bare-handed to save supplies

distractorExplanations.a: Raise the head of bed to a sitting position for bedpan use; long periods on the pan risk skin breakdown.
distractorExplanations.c: The pan sits under the buttocks so the opening is beneath the perineum; placed at the lower back it spills and misses.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are worn when removing and emptying the pan because it holds body fluids; bare-handed handling breaks Standard Precautions.

options.a: Output, since melted ice is excreted as urine
options.b: Not recorded, because ice chips are a solid
options.c: Intake (fluid intake) per facility protocol
options.d: Food intake, as a percentage of the meal tray

distractorExplanations.a: Ice chips are consumed, so they count toward intake; output covers urine, emesis, and drainage leaving the body.
distractorExplanations.b: Ice chips melt into water and count as fluid intake (often at about half their volume) even though they are served frozen.
distractorExplanations.d: Meal percentages track nutrition; ice chips belong in fluid intake on the I&O sheet, not in food intake.

options.a: Measure with shoes on and subtract one inch, reading the headpiece from below eye level
options.b: Have the patient stand with knees bent and chin down while lowering the headpiece firmly
options.c: Record the height the patient reports at admission instead of using the stadiometer
options.d: Have the patient stand straight without shoes and read the measurement at eye level

distractorExplanations.a: Height is measured without shoes rather than with an estimated subtraction, and the bar is read at eye level to avoid parallax.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients stand fully upright with heels together and head level; bent knees and a lowered chin understate height.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-reported height is often inaccurate; a measured stadiometer height is required when the order or protocol calls for it.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: Standardized technique yields accurate anthropometric data for care planning. Follow the facility measurement protocol.

options.a: Apply smoothly from toe upward, remove wrinkles, and follow size/order instructions
options.b: Apply after the patient has been up walking for an hour so the legs are warmed up
options.c: Fold the top band down a few inches if the stocking feels too long for the patient's leg
options.d: Choose a size by eye, pulling from the top of the thigh down to the toes to smooth it

distractorExplanations.b: TED hose go on before rising, while legs are elevated and least swollen; after walking, the legs are already edematous.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolled or folded tops act like a tourniquet and impair circulation; report a poor fit so the correct size is obtained.
distractorExplanations.d: Stockings are sized from leg measurements and applied from the toe upward; pulling downward bunches the fabric.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: Proper fit supports venous return; wrinkles and rolled tops can tourniquet and impair circulation. Do not roll the top down.

options.a: Measure standing first, then sitting, then lying, so the lowest pressure is recorded first
options.b: Follow the ordered sequence, support the patient, and record each set promptly
options.c: Have the patient stand quickly, and recheck only if they report feeling dizzy
options.d: Take each set back-to-back within 10 seconds so position changes do not alter results

distractorExplanations.a: Orthostatic checks start lying (after rest) and progress to sitting and standing; reversing the order defeats the comparison.
distractorExplanations.c: The patient rises with support and each position is measured at set intervals; waiting for dizziness misses silent drops.
distractorExplanations.d: Readings are taken after about 1–3 minutes in each position; the whole point is to capture position-related change.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: Orthostatic testing compares position changes; timing and support reduce fall risk. The usual sequence is lying, then sitting, then standing.

options.a: Positioning flat on the back, brushing firmly with a hard brush, and rinsing with a large cup of water
options.b: Doing the brushing for the patient even when they can hold the brush, to finish care more quickly
options.c: Positioning comfortably, using appropriate supplies, and reporting bleeding, pain, or swallow difficulty
options.d: Using full-strength alcohol mouthwash undiluted and charting a refusal without telling the nurse

distractorExplanations.a: Patients sit upright for oral care; flat positioning with large rinses risks aspiration, and hard, firm brushing injures gums.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients should do as much of their own care as they can to keep independence; the PCT assists only where needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol mouthwash dries and irritates oral tissue, and refusals or abnormal findings are reported to the nurse, not just charted.

options.a: At the nurses' station after collection, using the printed label from the requisition
options.b: Before collection, by pre-labeling the empty container at the bedside to save time
options.c: In the lab, where the specimen processor matches the cup with the requisition
options.d: At the bedside immediately using two identifiers per protocol before transport

distractorExplanations.a: Labeling away from the patient invites wrong-patient errors; specimens are labeled at the bedside in the patient's presence.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-labeled empty containers can end up used for the wrong patient; label after collection in front of the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: The collector, not the lab, labels the specimen; unlabeled specimens arriving in the lab are usually rejected.

options.a: Lock wheelchair/brake equipment, use proper body mechanics or a gait belt, and stay for safety
options.b: Place the commode at the foot of the bed facing away and have the patient walk to it unassisted
options.c: Position the commode on the patient's weaker side and pivot toward that side for balance
options.d: Lift the patient under the arms onto the commode, then step out without placing the call light

distractorExplanations.b: The commode goes beside the bed, angled toward the patient's strong side for a short pivot, with assistance as needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients transfer toward their stronger side; leading with the weak side increases fall risk during the pivot.
distractorExplanations.d: Lifting under the arms injures shoulders, and a patient left alone on a commode must have the call light within reach.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: Stable equipment and assisted transfers reduce falls during toileting. Use the gait belt as indicated.

options.a: Give small sips of water but no juice, since clear water is allowed under NPO
options.b: Give no oral fluids, reinforce the NPO order, and notify the nurse
options.c: Offer ice chips instead of water, since ice is not counted as oral intake under NPO
options.d: Let the patient drink the juice if the procedure is more than four hours away

distractorExplanations.a: NPO means nothing by mouth, including water, unless the provider writes an exception such as sips with medications.
distractorExplanations.c: Ice chips melt into fluid and are oral intake; they break NPO unless the provider specifically allows them.
distractorExplanations.d: PCTs cannot shorten NPO based on timing; only the provider changes fasting orders, and the nurse should be told.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: NPO means nothing by mouth unless a licensed clinician changes the order; PCTs do not override it or start IVs. Notify the nurse if the patient remains thirsty or distressed.

options.a: Have the patient exhale forcefully into the mouthpiece to raise the indicator
options.b: Encourage quick, sharp inhalations to raise the ball to the top as fast as possible
options.c: Encourage slow deep inhalations to target level and rest between attempts
options.d: Coach 10 breaths once daily with the patient lying flat to reduce fatigue

distractorExplanations.a: Incentive spirometers measure inhalation; blowing out into the device is a common error that does not expand the lungs.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid inhalations spike the flow indicator but do not sustain alveolar expansion; slow, deep, sustained breaths are the goal.
distractorExplanations.d: IS is typically used about 10 times every hour while awake, sitting upright; once daily lying flat is ineffective.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: IS coaching supports lung expansion post-op; shallow panting does not achieve ordered goals. Report inability to participate to the nurse.

options.a: Apply the stockings as ordered, then recheck the toes within an hour and report if unchanged
options.b: Elevate the legs on pillows above heart level and apply the stockings once color improves
options.c: Massage the toes and apply a warm heating pad to restore circulation before the stockings
options.d: Do not apply or tighten the stockings; report the cool, pale, painful toes to the nurse

distractorExplanations.a: Cool, pale, painful toes signal arterial compromise; compression is held and reported before application, not after.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevating ischemic legs further reduces arterial flow; with PAD signs the PCT holds the stockings and notifies the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Heating pads on ischemic feet can burn tissue with poor sensation, and massage does not fix arterial insufficiency.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-patient-care-02.explanation: Arterial insufficiency can be worsened by compression; circulatory warning signs need nursing review before applying TED hose. Report immediately.

options.a: Checked with a bath thermometer or wrist test per facility protocol to avoid scalding
options.b: Set by the patient's preference alone, since they can feel what is comfortable
options.c: Tested with the PCT's fingertips after the patient is already seated in the tub
options.d: Around 115–120°F (46–49°C) so the water stays warm through the entire bath

distractorExplanations.b: Older adults and patients with neuropathy may not sense scalding heat; staff verify temperature with a thermometer.
distractorExplanations.c: Fingertips are less sensitive than the wrist or a thermometer, and water is checked before the patient gets in.
distractorExplanations.d: Water above about 105–110°F can scald fragile skin; 115–120°F is too hot for patient bathing.

options.a: Silence the alarm and turn the pump off until the nurse can reconnect it at the next round
options.b: Reconnect only per protocol/training, ensure proper fit, and report persistent alarms to the nurse
options.c: Reconnect the tubing and tighten the sleeves so that two fingers cannot fit under them
options.d: Remove the sleeves and have the patient walk instead, since ambulation replaces the SCD order

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the SCD off without telling the nurse removes DVT prophylaxis for hours; report or fix per training right away.
distractorExplanations.c: SCD sleeves should allow about two fingers underneath; overtightening can impair circulation and injure skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Ambulation does not cancel an SCD order; only the provider changes it, and the nurse decides about removal.

options.a: Pull the pin (PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep)
options.b: Aim at the base of the fire (PASS step one)
options.c: Sound the alarm (RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain)
options.d: Squeeze the handle while sweeping side to side

distractorExplanations.b: Aiming at the base is the second PASS step; the pin must be pulled first or the handle will not discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: Alarm belongs to the RACE fire-response sequence, not to operating an extinguisher; PASS begins with Pull.
distractorExplanations.d: Squeeze and Sweep are the third and fourth PASS steps; without pulling the pin first the handle will not discharge.

options.a: A fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room for the patient
options.b: A surgical mask within 6 feet of the patient plus gloves for direct care
options.c: Gown and gloves for contact with the patient/environment as indicated
options.d: Gloves alone, with gowns reserved for when splashes of blood are expected

distractorExplanations.a: N95 respirators and negative pressure are airborne precautions (TB, measles); contact precautions use gown and gloves.
distractorExplanations.b: A mask within about 6 feet is the droplet-precaution rule (e.g., influenza); contact precautions require gown and gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Gowns for expected splashes is a Standard Precautions rule; contact precautions add a gown for any patient/environment contact.

options.a: Secure a confused patient to the chair to prevent unassisted standing
options.b: Lift a fully dependent patient from bed to chair without a mechanical lift
options.c: Pull the patient up in bed by the belt when repositioning toward the headboard
options.d: Assist transfer/ambulation safely by providing a secure hold

distractorExplanations.a: Using a gait belt to keep a patient seated makes it a restraint, which requires a provider order and monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Dependent patients who cannot bear weight need a mechanical lift; a gait belt only guides patients who can help.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving a patient up in bed uses a lift sheet and two staff; pulling on a gait belt causes shear and injury.

options.a: Red biohazard bags for infectious waste
options.b: Puncture-resistant sharps containers
options.c: Recapped, then placed in the regular trash
options.d: Any rigid container once it is filled to the top

distractorExplanations.a: Red bags are for soft blood-soaked waste; needles can puncture bags, so sharps go in rigid puncture-resistant containers.
distractorExplanations.c: Needles are not recapped by hand and do not go in regular trash; they go directly into a sharps container.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharps containers are approved puncture-resistant units replaced at the fill line (about three-quarters full); overfilling causes sticks.

options.a: A family member's written consent and a check on the patient at least once per shift
options.b: A nurse's verbal approval and tying the restraint to the side rail with a quick-release knot
options.c: A provider order (except true emergencies per policy) and frequent monitoring/documentation
options.d: A provider order renewed weekly and release of the restraint for toileting every 8 hours

distractorExplanations.a: Restraints need a provider order, not family consent, and are checked far more often than once per shift.
distractorExplanations.b: Restraints are tied to the bed frame, not side rails, which move and can injure; a provider order is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Restraint orders are renewed far more often than weekly, and release for toileting and skin care is about every 2 hours.

options.a: Patients with a confirmed bloodborne infection
options.b: All patients, regardless of known infection status
options.c: Patients on contact, droplet, or airborne isolation
options.d: Any patient with visible blood or open wounds

distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions are not limited to known HIV/HBV/HCV cases; infection status is often unknown, so they apply to everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation categories are Transmission-Based Precautions layered on top of Standard Precautions, which apply to every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions apply before blood is visible; any patient's blood, body fluids, or non-intact skin may be infectious.

options.a: Wrap the frayed area with electrical tape and report it at the end of the shift
options.b: Keep using it if it passes a quick power-on test, then note it in the shift report
options.c: Remove it from service, tag/report per policy, and do not use until repaired
options.d: Unplug it by pulling the cord and move it to the patient's bathroom for storage

distractorExplanations.a: Tape is not an approved repair; a damaged cord is a shock and fire hazard, so the device leaves service immediately.
distractorExplanations.b: Powering on does not prove the insulation is intact; frayed cords are removed from service until biomed repairs them.
distractorExplanations.d: Pull the plug, not the cord, and do not store electrical equipment in wet areas; tag it and send it for repair.

options.a: They replace hourly rounding once activated, so checks can be spaced out
options.b: They let staff leave the bed in high position since the alarm will sound
options.c: They count as a restraint, so a provider order is needed before use
options.d: They are adjuncts—respond promptly and continue other fall precautions

distractorExplanations.a: Bed alarms alert staff after a patient moves; they do not replace hourly rounding, toileting, and other fall precautions.
distractorExplanations.b: The bed stays in the lowest position with brakes locked; an alarm sounds only after the patient is already getting up.
distractorExplanations.c: Bed alarms do not restrict movement, so they are not restraints and do not require a restraint order.

options.a: Applying loosely at the chest over the gown so the patient can breathe comfortably
options.b: Applying snugly at the waist over clothing and holding the belt to guide/support
options.c: Applying snugly at the waist and lifting a dependent patient by the belt alone
options.d: Applying at the waist directly on bare skin and holding it with a fingertip grip

distractorExplanations.a: Gait belts go snugly around the waist, not loosely at the chest; a loose belt slides up and gives no secure hold.
distractorExplanations.c: The belt guides patients who can bear weight; fully dependent patients need a mechanical lift and more staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Belts go over clothing to protect the skin, and staff use a firm underhand grip on the belt for a secure hold.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-safety-infectio.explanation: Gait belts aid safe ambulation/transfers with proper technique and adequate assistance. Do not lift heavy dependent patients by the belt alone without help.

options.a: Remove the gown and gloves, and skip hand hygiene if the hands look clean
options.b: Remove PPE in the hallway after leaving the room so the room stays uncontaminated
options.c: Remove contaminated PPE carefully to avoid self-contamination, then perform hand hygiene
options.d: Use alcohol gel on gloved hands and keep the same gloves on for the next patient

distractorExplanations.a: Hand hygiene is required after PPE removal even when hands look clean, because gloves can have micro-tears.
distractorExplanations.b: PPE for contact precautions is removed at the doorway before leaving so contaminated items stay inside the room.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are single-use and changed between patients; sanitizing gloved hands does not make the gloves safe to reuse.

options.a: No smoking within the room, though e-cigarettes are permitted at the bedside
options.b: Petroleum jelly on the lips and nostrils to prevent dryness from the cannula
options.c: Wool blankets in place of cotton to keep the patient warm during oxygen use
options.d: No smoking, sparks, or open flames near oxygen sources per policy

distractorExplanations.a: E-cigarettes and vape devices are ignition sources too; they are prohibited wherever oxygen is in use.
distractorExplanations.b: Petroleum-based products are flammable in oxygen-rich air; use water-based lubricants for dry lips and nares.
distractorExplanations.c: Wool and synthetics generate static sparks; cotton is preferred around oxygen to reduce ignition risk.

options.d: Covering it with a towel and waiting for housekeeping, with no warning sign posted

options.c: Mask first, then gloves, then gown with the gown cuffs pulled over the gloves

options.d: Cut the extra tubing to shorten it and reconnect it with tape

nha-cpct-readiness-check-safety-infectio.explanation: Proper routing and equipment checks reduce fall risk for patients and staff. Report excessive tubing length to the nurse.

options.a: A surgical mask for staff within 6 feet of the patient and a private room with the door left open

options.a: EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant (e.g., bleach-based per policy)
options.b: Alcohol-based wipes on high-touch surfaces, as for routine room cleaning
options.c: Quaternary ammonium disinfectant, the standard choice for MRSA rooms
options.d: Hand hygiene gel spread on bed rails and tables after the patient leaves

distractorExplanations.d: Hand gel is not a surface disinfectant and alcohol cannot kill spores; use an EPA-registered sporicidal product.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-safety-infectio.explanation: Spores survive routine alcohol cleaning; sporicidal agents are used on surfaces per protocol. Alcohol rub alone is not adequate on surfaces.

options.a: Recap it with both hands, then carry it to the sharps container at the nurses' station
options.b: Activate the safety device immediately and place it in a sharps container
options.c: Unscrew the needle from the holder by hand and drop just the needle in the sharps box
options.d: Set it on the tray and activate the safety device after bandaging the patient's arm

distractorExplanations.d: The safety device is engaged immediately after withdrawal; setting an exposed needle down risks a stick.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-safety-infectio.explanation: Two-handed recapping is a classic needlestick risk; engage the safety feature and discard in a puncture-resistant container. Do not recap with two hands.

options.a: Using two identifiers (e.g., name and DOB) matching the order/wristband
options.b: Asking 'Are you Ms. Lee?' and confirming the room and bed on the order

options.d: Using the name and room number from the requisition, compared with the chart

options.a: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
options.b: Fifth intercostal space, anterior axillary line
options.c: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
options.d: Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line

distractorExplanations.b: The 5th ICS anterior axillary line is V5; V4 is at the midclavicular line on the same horizontal level.
distractorExplanations.c: The 4th ICS at the left sternal border is V2; V4 is at the 5th ICS in the left midclavicular line.

options.a: Warming the patient and ensuring relaxed muscles/good electrode contact
options.b: Turning on the 60-Hz filter, since shivering is a type of electrical interference
options.c: Asking the patient to grip the bed rails firmly to keep the arms still
options.d: Increasing the gain to 20 mm/mV so the waveforms stand out from the artifact

distractorExplanations.b: The 60-Hz filter targets AC electrical interference; somatic tremor from shivering is reduced by warming and relaxation.
distractorExplanations.c: Gripping tenses the muscles and increases somatic artifact; the arms should rest relaxed at the patient's sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubling the gain enlarges the artifact along with the complexes; it does not remove muscle tremor.

options.a: Hemolysis from slow tube filling
options.b: Additive carryover between tubes
options.c: Clotting in the lavender EDTA tube
options.d: Hemoconcentration from the tourniquet

distractorExplanations.a: Hemolysis comes from technique (small needles, shaking); order of draw prevents additive cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Clotting in EDTA tubes is prevented by prompt gentle inversion, not by the sequence in which tubes are filled.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemoconcentration is caused by leaving the tourniquet on longer than about 1 minute, not by tube sequence.

options.a: Hemodilution and falsely decreased protein levels
options.b: Clotting in the needle and a falsely low platelet count
options.c: Hemoconcentration and falsely elevated analytes
options.d: Glycolysis and falsely decreased glucose results

distractorExplanations.a: Prolonged venous stasis concentrates proteins and cells; it causes hemoconcentration, not dilution.
distractorExplanations.b: Tourniquet time affects analyte concentration; clotting in the needle relates to slow fills and poor technique.
distractorExplanations.d: Falsely low glucose comes from delayed processing (glycolysis), not tourniquet time; stasis raises analytes.

options.a: Apply standard electrodes but remove them within 5 minutes of the tracing
options.b: Postpone the EKG until the provider changes the order to a rhythm strip
options.c: Apply a thin layer of lotion under each electrode to protect the skin
options.d: Use alternative electrodes/skins preps per policy and document allergy

distractorExplanations.a: Even short contact can trigger an adhesive reaction; hypoallergenic electrodes are used for allergic patients.
distractorExplanations.b: An allergy does not change the test ordered; adapt the electrodes per policy and notify the nurse if unsure.
distractorExplanations.c: Lotion under electrodes blocks conduction and causes artifact; it does not prevent an adhesive reaction.

options.a: Finish filling the current tube quickly, then remove the needle and tourniquet
options.b: Stop the draw and protect the patient from injury (lower head/supine)
options.c: Have the patient sit up straight and take deep breaths before continuing
options.d: Apply an ammonia inhalant right away to keep the patient awake for the draw

distractorExplanations.a: At the first sign of syncope the tourniquet and needle come out immediately; continuing risks injury if the patient falls.
distractorExplanations.c: Sitting upright worsens cerebral blood flow during fainting; lower the head or lay the patient down.
distractorExplanations.d: Ammonia inhalants are discouraged in many policies because of airway risk; stop the draw and position safely.

options.a: Verify the order, identify the patient, and squeeze the finger hard to get a large drop
options.b: Clean the fingertip with alcohol and puncture right away, before the alcohol has dried
options.c: Verify the order/protocol, identify the patient, and ensure the meter/strips are in date
options.d: Choose the center of the index finger pad and run quality control once a month

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing ('milking') the finger adds tissue fluid and hemolysis, falsely changing glucose; let blood flow freely.
distractorExplanations.b: Wet alcohol dilutes the sample and stings; let the site air-dry completely before the puncture.
distractorExplanations.d: Punctures go on the side of the fingertip pad of the middle or ring finger; QC is run daily or per manufacturer.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-phlebotomy-ekg-.explanation: POCT accuracy and safety depend on ID, valid supplies, and skin prep; lancets are single-use. Meter and strips must also be appropriate for the test.

options.a: Cleanse as directed, void a small amount, then collect midstream into a sterile container
options.b: Collect the first part of the stream into the sterile cup, then finish in the toilet
options.c: Cleanse as directed, then pour the first morning void from a clean bedpan into a cup
options.d: Void the midstream portion into a clean, non-sterile cup and cap it within the hour

distractorExplanations.b: First-stream urine flushes urethral bacteria; culture specimens use the midstream portion to avoid contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Bedpan urine is non-sterile; culture specimens are collected midstream directly into the sterile container.
distractorExplanations.d: Culture specimens need a sterile container; a clean non-sterile cup can introduce bacteria and false growth.

options.a: Apply a warm compress and elevate the arm, then report it at the next scheduled round
options.b: Stop involving the site per scope—do not adjust rates—and report immediately to the nurse
options.c: Clamp the IV tubing and remove the tape to inspect the insertion site more closely
options.d: Lower the IV bag below the site to check for blood return before telling the nurse

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing warm or cold compresses is a nursing decision after assessment, and infiltration needs immediate reporting.
distractorExplanations.c: Clamping lines and handling IV dressings are outside PCT scope; report the swollen, cool site to the nurse right away.
distractorExplanations.d: Checking for blood return is a nursing assessment; PCTs do not manipulate IV lines and report infiltration signs first.

options.a: Fourth intercostal space right sternal border
options.b: Fifth intercostal space, midaxillary line (left)
options.c: Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line (left)
options.d: Midway between V2 and V4 on the left chest

distractorExplanations.b: The 5th ICS midaxillary line is V6; V4 is at the midclavicular line on the same horizontal level.
distractorExplanations.d: The point midway between V2 and V4 is V3; V4 itself sits at the 5th ICS in the left midclavicular line.
distractorExplanations.a: That is V1.

options.a: Speed clotting by shaking the tube firmly 10 times
options.b: Release trapped air so the tube fills to the line
options.c: Separate serum from cells before centrifugation
options.d: Mix additive with blood without causing hemolysis

distractorExplanations.a: Shaking hemolyzes red cells; even clot-activator tubes are inverted gently, about 5 times, not shaken.
distractorExplanations.b: Fill volume is set by the tube's vacuum; inversion mixes the additive and does not change the fill level.
distractorExplanations.c: Separation happens during centrifugation after clotting; inversion only mixes the additive with the blood.

options.a: Coated with a thin layer of lotion to improve conduction under each pad
options.b: Shaved over every electrode site on all patients before applying the pads
options.c: Cleaned of oils/lotion and dried to improve adhesion and reduce artifact
options.d: Wiped with alcohol and the electrodes applied while the skin is still wet

distractorExplanations.a: Lotion increases impedance and lifts electrodes; skin should be clean and dry, not moisturized.
distractorExplanations.b: Hair is clipped where it prevents contact, not shaved routinely on every patient; shaving causes nicks and irritation.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol must dry fully before electrodes go on; wet skin reduces adhesion and causes artifact.

options.a: 5 mm/s, used for routine rhythm strips at the bedside
options.b: 10 mm/s, matching the standard 10 mm/mV gain setting
options.c: 12.5 mm/s unless a faster speed is specifically ordered
options.d: 25 mm/s unless a different speed is specifically ordered

distractorExplanations.a: 5 mm/s is not a standard recording speed; routine 12-leads and rhythm strips run at 25 mm/s.
distractorExplanations.b: 10 mm/mV is the standard gain (amplitude) calibration, not the paper speed; routine speed is 25 mm/s.
distractorExplanations.c: 12.5 mm/s is a rarely used half-speed option; the routine default is 25 mm/s, with 50 mm/s for fast rates.

options.a: Lies close to arteries and nerves, increasing injury risk
options.b: Is the most superficial vein and collapses easily
options.c: Lies on the lateral thumb side, where hematomas form most
options.d: Contains valves that cause hemolysis in most tubes

distractorExplanations.b: The median cubital is the most superficial, well-anchored vein; the basilic is avoided for its nerve and artery proximity.
distractorExplanations.c: The lateral (thumb-side) vein is the cephalic, a second choice; the basilic is medial, near the brachial artery.
distractorExplanations.d: Valves can impede flow but do not cause hemolysis in tubes; the basilic is last choice because of nearby nerves and artery.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-phlebotomy-ekg-.explanation: Medial antecubital basilic proximity to the brachial artery/nerve favors cephalic/median preference. The risk is highest in inexperienced hands.

options.a: On the central back curve of the heel, after warming, using a 2.4 mm adult lancet
options.b: Only per facility protocol/training, using appropriate lancet depth/site and warming
options.c: On the medial or lateral heel, squeezing firmly and continuously to speed blood flow
options.d: On the side of the middle fingertip, as for adults, after warming the infant's hand

distractorExplanations.a: The posterior heel curvature overlies bone; punctures go on the medial or lateral plantar surface with depth of 2.0 mm or less.
distractorExplanations.c: The site is right, but constant firm squeezing causes hemolysis and tissue-fluid contamination; use gentle intermittent pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Infant fingersticks risk hitting bone; infants under about 1 year get heel sticks, not fingersticks.

options.a: Hemodilution, falsely lowering potassium and calcium results
options.b: Faster clotting that prevents adequate tube fill volume
options.c: Hemolysis and hemoconcentration, falsely affecting some results
options.d: Vein collapse, so a smaller butterfly needle becomes required

distractorExplanations.b: Fist pumping alters analyte levels through muscle activity and hemolysis; it does not cause clotting that blocks tube fill.
distractorExplanations.d: Vein collapse comes from excessive vacuum or small veins, not pumping; pumping's main effect is falsely raised potassium.

options.a: Redirect the needle sideways under the skin to find the vein
options.b: Keep the tourniquet on and try again in the same arm right away
options.c: Make up to four more attempts before notifying the nurse
options.d: Release tourniquet, apply pressure, and follow facility policy

distractorExplanations.b: The tourniquet is released after a failed attempt; leaving it on beyond 1 minute causes hemoconcentration.
distractorExplanations.c: Most policies allow two attempts per collector before escalating; four more attempts traumatizes the patient.

options.b: Inverted complexes in V1 and V2 with normal limb leads throughout the tracing
options.c: Low-voltage, flat complexes in the chest leads with 60-cycle interference lines
options.d: A wandering baseline in each lead that rises and falls with the patient's breathing

distractorExplanations.d: Baseline wander with breathing is respiratory artifact from poor contact, not limb-electrode reversal.

options.a: Fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (left side)
options.b: Fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line (left side)
options.c: Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.d: Fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line (left side)

distractorExplanations.a: The 5th ICS anterior axillary line is V5; V6 is further lateral at the midaxillary line on the same level.
distractorExplanations.c: The 4th ICS at the left sternal border is V2; V6 is lateral at the 5th ICS midaxillary line.
distractorExplanations.d: The 5th ICS midclavicular line is V4; V6 sits two landmarks lateral at the midaxillary line.

options.a: 60-cycle AC interference from nearby electrical equipment
options.b: Somatic tremor from muscle tension or shivering in the patient's arms and legs
options.c: Respiratory movement altering electrode contact (respiratory artifact)
options.d: Limb lead reversal between the right and left arm electrodes

options.a: Pour blood from an overfilled tube of a different color into it until it reaches the fill line
options.b: Ask the lab to run the test anyway since EDTA tubes do not need a full draw
options.c: Draw a second lavender tube and combine both partial tubes into one sample
options.d: Report the event, document per policy, and recollect if ordered—QNS may reject testing

options.a: On the torso/shoulder area per facility protocol to approximate limb lead positions
options.b: On the chest lead positions V1 and V6, reusing those electrodes for the limb leads
options.c: On the stumps at different heights on each side so the leads can be told apart

options.c: Switch the monitor to a different lead and continue without reporting

options.a: Access any chart on the unit as long as it is not shared outside
options.b: Access only the minimum necessary PHI for their job duties
options.c: Share PHI with family members who visit the patient
options.d: Obtain written consent before sharing PHI with the care team

options.a: Respecting beliefs/preferences and using interpreters when language barriers exist

options.d: Assuming a patient's food and care preferences based on their ethnic background

options.a: Erase the entry neatly and rewrite it so the record looks clean and legible
options.b: Correct per facility policy (e.g., single line, initial, date)
options.c: Black out the error with a marker so it cannot be misread, then initial it
options.d: Write the correction in the margin without initials so it does not draw attention

distractorExplanations.a: Erasing obliterates the original entry and looks like tampering; draw a single line, initial, and date.
distractorExplanations.c: Blacking out hides the original text; corrections must leave the original readable under a single line.
distractorExplanations.d: Corrections must be dated and initialed to show who made them and when; unsigned margin edits are improper.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Legal records must show transparent corrections. Do not erase or obliterate the original entry.

options.a: Access to their own chart directly from the PCT on request at any time
options.b: Choosing which staff member is assigned to them on every shift
options.c: Privacy, respectful care, and involvement in care decisions as applicable
options.d: Receiving any treatment they request, even if the provider has not ordered it

distractorExplanations.a: Patients access records through the facility's formal process, not by the PCT handing over the chart.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients can raise concerns about caregivers, but they do not have a right to choose staff assignments.
distractorExplanations.d: Patients may refuse treatment, but they cannot demand treatments a provider has not ordered or judged appropriate.

options.a: Reporting directly to human resources first, before speaking with the coworker
options.b: Raising it during shift report in front of the whole team so everyone hears both sides
options.c: Avoiding the coworker and asking the charge nurse to change your assignments
options.d: Addressing privately and professionally, then involving supervisor if unresolved/safety issue

distractorExplanations.a: Most minor conflicts start with a private conversation; HR is escalation for unresolved or serious issues.
distractorExplanations.b: Public discussion during report embarrasses staff and distracts from patient handoff; address it privately.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoidance leaves the conflict unresolved and can affect patient care; talk to the coworker first.

options.a: Document unusual events for quality improvement and risk management
options.b: Record disciplinary action against the staff member involved in the event
options.c: Replace the clinical note so the event is not mentioned in the patient chart
options.d: Notify the patient's family and insurer of every staff error in writing

distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are non-punitive tools for finding system problems, not disciplinary records.
distractorExplanations.c: The chart still records the facts and care given; the incident report is filed separately, not as a substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Incident reports are internal, confidential QI documents; disclosure to families follows a separate process.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Follow facility policy on what goes in chart vs incident system. Incident reports are not typically filed in the patient chart as a progress-note substitute.

options.a: Are required by HIPAA as part of the privacy rule
options.b: Support patient trust, infection control, and team reliability
options.c: Determine eligibility for NHA certification renewal
options.d: Mainly affect how patients rate the hospital food service

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA governs the privacy of health information; dress codes and attendance come from facility policy.
distractorExplanations.c: NHA renewal depends on continuing education credits and fees, not workplace appearance or punctuality.
distractorExplanations.d: Appearance and punctuality affect trust, safety, and staffing coverage, not food-service satisfaction.

options.a: Share the diagnosis if the visitor can correctly state the patient's full date of birth
options.b: Give a general summary of the diagnosis without using medical terms
options.c: Decline to share PHI and direct them to the appropriate authorized process/nurse
options.d: Ask the visitor to sign the visitor log, then share the diagnosis

distractorExplanations.a: Knowing a DOB does not prove authorization; disclosure depends on the patient's consent or an approved process.
distractorExplanations.b: A plain-language summary is still PHI disclosure; PCTs do not explain diagnoses to unauthorized visitors.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing in for visitation does not authorize PHI access; refer to the nurse and the patient's wishes.

options.a: Accepting small gifts quietly so the patient's family does not feel rejected
options.b: Sharing your personal phone number so the patient can reach you after discharge
options.c: Friending patients on social media to support them after they go home
options.d: Keeping relationships therapeutic and not exchanging romantic advances with patients

distractorExplanations.a: Gifts are handled per facility policy, usually declined or reported; secret acceptance blurs boundaries.
distractorExplanations.b: Personal contact after discharge creates a dual relationship; patients use the facility's channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Social media connections with patients cross professional boundaries and risk PHI exposure.

options.a: Correct it according to facility policy (e.g., amendment) without erasing the original
options.b: Rewrite the whole page from memory and shred the original so the record is neat
options.c: Ask the nurse to delete the electronic entry and re-enter it under your login
options.d: Add a late entry backdated to the original time so the timeline looks correct

distractorExplanations.b: Destroying the original and recreating the page is falsification; the original must stay in the record.
distractorExplanations.c: EHR entries are amended with an audit trail, not deleted; deleting removes legal evidence of the original.
distractorExplanations.d: Late entries carry the actual current date and time and are labeled late; backdating is falsification.

options.a: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan in a progress note
options.b: Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation/Request
options.c: Symptoms, Baseline, Allergies, and Response to treatment
options.d: Safety, Behavior, Activity, and Rest observations for the shift

distractorExplanations.a: Subjective/Objective/Assessment/Plan is SOAP charting, not the SBAR verbal communication format.
distractorExplanations.c: In SBAR the B is Background and the A is Assessment; Symptoms/Baseline/Allergies/Response is not the SBAR structure.
distractorExplanations.d: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; it is a communication format, not an observation checklist.

options.a: Calm the visitor alone in a private room away from other patients
options.b: Restrain the visitor physically until security arrives on the unit
options.c: Prioritize safety, remove self/patients from harm, and call security
options.d: Finish care for the current patient, then report it at the end of shift

distractorExplanations.a: De-escalating in an isolated room removes help and exits; stay in view of others near an exit and call security.
distractorExplanations.b: Staff should not physically restrain visitors; trained security or police manage threats while staff stay safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Credible threats need an immediate security response; waiting until end of shift leaves everyone at risk.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Safety systems and de-escalation/security response protect everyone. Follow the facility's violence-response procedure.

options.a: Ask the family member directly about the injuries before deciding to report
options.b: Wait until there is clear proof of abuse before making any report
options.c: Document the injuries in the chart and bring them up at next week's care plan conference
options.d: Report to the nurse/supervisor and follow mandated reporter and facility policy promptly

distractorExplanations.a: Questioning the suspected abuser can endanger the patient; report suspicions without investigating yourself.
distractorExplanations.b: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion; proof is not required and investigators determine the facts.
distractorExplanations.c: Charting is needed, but suspected abuse must be reported promptly, not held for a later conference.

options.a: A HIPAA violation and unprofessional conduct subject to discipline
options.b: Acceptable if the patient's face is blurred or cropped out
options.c: Permitted when the patient gives verbal permission at the bedside
options.d: Allowed if the account is private and limited to close friends

distractorExplanations.b: Tattoos, rooms, wristbands, or context can still identify the patient; blurring does not make the post permissible.
distractorExplanations.c: Disclosure needs written authorization under facility policy, and personal social media posting is usually prohibited anyway.
distractorExplanations.d: Private accounts still disclose PHI to people without a need to know; privacy settings do not cure the breach.

options.a: Accept it but donate the cash to the unit's staff fund afterward
options.b: Politely decline and report the gift per facility policy
options.c: Accept small amounts under $20 since nominal gifts are allowed
options.d: Decline the cash but provide the extra favors to keep the patient happy

distractorExplanations.a: Accepting cash for favors still creates an obligation; donating it later does not fix the boundary problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Some policies allow token non-cash gifts, but cash offered for extra favors is declined and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Preferential care for one patient is itself a boundary problem; care follows the plan, and the offer is reported.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Gifts can create undue influence and boundary violations; follow policy on declining/reporting. Declining and reporting maintains professional boundaries.

options.a: Explain the diagnosis simply using the patient's discharge paperwork
options.b: Translate if the PCT is fluent, since fluency qualifies as interpreting
options.c: Not independently explain or translate the diagnosis; notify the nurse
options.d: Ask the patient's bilingual teenager to translate the physician's notes

distractorExplanations.a: Explaining a diagnosis is a licensed clinician task even with paperwork in hand; the PCT notifies the nurse.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluency is not interpreter qualification; medical interpreting requires trained, qualified interpreters.
distractorExplanations.d: Family members, especially minors, are not qualified medical interpreters and may omit or distort information.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Explaining a diagnosis is a licensed-clinician task. PCTs escalate and use qualified interpreters for role-appropriate talk—they do not ad-lib medical translations. Use a qualified interpreter only for communication within the PCT role.

options.a: Call security to keep the patient on the unit until the physician arrives to approve it
options.b: Help the patient pack and walk them out, since competent adults may leave at any time
options.c: Have the patient sign the AMA form with the PCT as witness, then notify the nurse
options.d: Notify the nurse immediately so AMA process, education, and documentation can occur

distractorExplanations.a: A competent adult can leave AMA; holding them with security without legal grounds is false imprisonment.
distractorExplanations.b: Competent patients can leave, but the nurse must be told first so AMA education and the form are completed.
distractorExplanations.c: The AMA discussion and form are handled by the nurse or provider; the PCT notifies the nurse before any form.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: AMA workflows are nursing/provider responsibilities; PCTs escalate promptly. Follow facility AMA policy.

options.a: Not accept or carry out the verbal medication order; notify the nurse
options.b: Write down the order, read it back, and give it to the nurse to carry out
options.c: Accept the order since the provider gave it directly, then tell the nurse
options.d: Give the dose if it is already in the patient's medication drawer

distractorExplanations.b: Read-back is how licensed nurses take verbal orders; PCTs do not receive medication orders at all.
distractorExplanations.c: A direct call from the provider does not make the PCT a licensed receiver of medication orders.
distractorExplanations.d: Medication administration is outside PCT scope whatever is stocked; the nurse receives and gives the dose.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: PCTs do not take verbal medication orders, administer meds, or prescribe. Licensed nurses receive and transcribe orders. A licensed nurse receives the order.

options.a: Explain the EKG findings briefly since the PCT recorded the tracing
options.b: Not diagnose or interpret results for treatment; notify the nurse
options.c: Reassure the patient that the results look normal so they stay calm
options.d: Tell the patient to ask the doctor tomorrow and continue with other tasks

distractorExplanations.a: Recording an EKG does not authorize interpretation; explaining results belongs to the nurse or provider.
distractorExplanations.c: Saying results are normal is still interpretation and may be false reassurance; refer the question to the nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: A patient worried about a heart attack needs the nurse notified now; delaying may miss real cardiac symptoms.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Result interpretation and treatment changes are licensed-clinician duties. PCTs report the question and any distress—they do not diagnose. Stay with the patient if they are distressed.

options.a: Acceptable if the coworker is in the parking lot and arrives soon
options.b: A minor policy issue handled by a verbal reminder from HR
options.c: Time fraud and grounds for disciplinary action including termination
options.d: Allowed if the charge nurse approves it during short staffing

distractorExplanations.a: Any punch for someone not present falsifies time records; being nearby does not change that.
distractorExplanations.b: Buddy punching is payroll fraud, typically leading to serious discipline or termination, not just a reminder.
distractorExplanations.d: No supervisor can authorize falsified time records; late arrivals are documented accurately.

options.a: Follow the family's verbal wishes when they differ from the written directive
options.b: Explain the directive's meaning to the patient when they ask about it
options.c: Help the patient update the directive by writing in their new wishes
options.d: Know where it is documented and report questions or changes to the nurse

distractorExplanations.a: Family disagreements are referred to the nurse or provider; the PCT does not override the written directive.
distractorExplanations.b: Explaining a legal and medical directive is beyond PCT scope; questions go to the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Changes to advance directives require a formal legal process; PCTs report requests to the nurse.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Advance directives guide licensed providers; PCTs support locating and communicating concerns. Do not interpret legal wishes independently.

options.a: Receive orientation to equipment, assignments, and emergency procedures
options.b: Follow the home unit's procedures, since policies are standard across units
options.c: Accept each task assigned, since float staff cannot decline assignments
options.d: Review only the patient list and skip the emergency equipment locations

distractorExplanations.b: Units differ in equipment, layouts, and protocols; a floated PCT needs the receiving unit's orientation.
distractorExplanations.c: Float staff can and should decline tasks outside their training and inform the charge nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: Knowing crash cart, exit, and alarm locations is a core part of float orientation, not an optional step.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Orientation reduces errors; unfamiliar procedures require supervision. Ask questions before accepting unfamiliar tasks.

options.a: Wait to report until the harassment happens at least three more times
options.b: Document objectively and report through HR/supervisor per facility anti-harassment policy
options.c: Confront the coworker publicly at the nurses' station so others see the behavior stop
options.d: Report it to the state nursing board rather than to the facility's HR department

distractorExplanations.a: Harassment should be reported when it occurs; policies do not require a pattern of repeated incidents.
distractorExplanations.c: Public confrontation can escalate conflict; use the formal reporting channel through supervisor or HR.
distractorExplanations.d: Workplace harassment goes through the facility's policy channel (supervisor/HR), not a licensing board.

options.a: Hold charting until the system is restored, then enter it from memory
options.b: Record care on personal notes and phone photos to upload later
options.c: Follow the facility downtime plan for paper documentation and orders
options.d: Use the paper forms and shred them once the system is back online

distractorExplanations.a: Delayed charting from memory loses accuracy; downtime plans use paper forms in real time.
distractorExplanations.b: Personal notes and phone photos of PHI are not approved records and risk privacy breaches.
distractorExplanations.d: Downtime paper records are scanned or entered and retained per policy; shredding destroys the legal record.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Downtime plans maintain continuity and legal record integrity. The plan also covers medication workflows.

options.a: Sign as a witness after reading the will
options.b: Ask another PCT to sign as the witness
options.c: Have the patient's roommate witness it
options.d: Decline politely and notify the nurse

distractorExplanations.a: Witnessing legal documents is outside the PCT role and policy; reading the will first does not make it appropriate.
distractorExplanations.b: Passing the request to another PCT does not fix the problem; facility policy routes it through the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Arranging witnesses is not the PCT's role, and involving a roommate exposes the patient's private information.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Legal witnessing has specific requirements and is not a nursing assistant duty. Witnessing legal documents is outside PCT scope and policy.

options.a: Report concerns through chain of command and document objectively
options.b: Refuse the assignment and leave the unit after telling the charge nurse
options.c: Post about the unsafe staffing on social media to pressure management
options.d: Call the state health department before telling the charge nurse

distractorExplanations.b: Leaving after accepting an assignment is patient abandonment; report concerns while continuing care.
distractorExplanations.c: Public posts bypass the chain of command and risk exposing patient or facility information.
distractorExplanations.d: External reporting is a later step; concerns start with the charge nurse and the chain of command.

nha-cpct-readiness-check-professional-pr.explanation: Advocacy uses proper channels; abandonment worsens safety. Do not abandon patients while concerns are addressed.

options.a: Sign it, since the nurse is responsible for any entry made under the nurse's direction
options.b: Refuse to falsify documentation and report the request to supervision per policy
options.c: Sign only if the nurse confirms the care was done by someone else
options.d: Refuse to sign but keep the request to yourself to avoid conflict

distractorExplanations.a: Each person is accountable for their own signature; signing for care not performed is falsification.
distractorExplanations.c: Documentation reflects care you personally performed; you cannot sign for another person's work.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusing is right, but a request to falsify records must also be reported to supervision.
